passage: I'm Tanvir. Last year, at twenty, I forwarded a video to our family group showing "proof" that a neighbourhood near ours was dangerous. It had dramatic music, angry captions and no date. My uncle Bhupen replied, "Where is this from?" I didn't know. He found the original: it was from another country, five years old. I felt stupid, but mostly I felt used. The video had wanted me angry, and it worked. Since then I check three things before I share: who made it, when, and what it wants me to feel. I also started reading one article a week from people I usually disagree with. Some of them make better points than I expected.

qa.q: What did Uncle Bhupen ask about the video?
qa.a: "Where is this from?"

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel after learning the video was old and foreign?
qa.a: Tanvir felt stupid and used, realising the video was designed to provoke anger.

qa.q: What habit is Tanvir now using, and why does it help?
qa.a: Checking who made it, when and what it wants Tanvir to feel, because it catches manipulation before sharing.

qa.q: How might Uncle Bhupen have felt asking his question?
qa.a: Probably concerned but calm, wanting to correct the record without humiliating anyone.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to spot emotional manipulation and misinformation, and to read opposing views fairly.

passage:
Lecturer's note, Uday, Media Studies, October
Nilesh (20) presented his analysis of election posters from two rival parties this week. He didn't pick a side. He showed how both used the same tricks: fear-words, crowd photos, one enemy to blame. He also pointed out a fact on one poster that was true but missing its context. When a classmate accused him of "defending the other side", he said calmly, "I'm checking both the same way." I've asked him to turn it into a short workshop for first-years and suggested a reading list on propaganda history.

qa.q: What did Nilesh analyse?
qa.a: Election posters from two rival parties.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have felt when accused of defending the other side?
qa.a: He may have felt a flash of irritation, but stayed calm and confident in his fair method.

qa.q: Why is Uday's workshop suggestion a good next step?
qa.a: It spreads Nilesh's even-handed approach and gives first-years a practical way to spot manipulation.

qa.q: How might the classmate who accused Nilesh see things later?
qa.a: He or she might realise that checking both sides equally isn't taking a side.

grounding: Shows a young adult identifying propaganda techniques on both sides fairly, noted by his lecturer.

passage:
Karthik's diary, Tuesday
Argued with Payal at the canteen about a viral post saying migrants are taking all the jobs in our city. I was sure it was true; the numbers looked official. Payal asked, "Which numbers, from where?" I couldn't say. Tonight I looked it up. The chart in the post cut off half the years and had no source. The real employment data was more complicated. Then I read an interview with a migrant worker who builds half the flats in our area. I still have questions, but I was angry because the post wanted me angry. Tomorrow I'll tell Payal she was right to ask.

qa.q: What was missing from the chart in the post?
qa.a: It cut off half the years and had no source.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel after checking the facts?
qa.a: Karthik felt humbled and a bit uneasy, realising the anger had been stirred on purpose.

qa.q: What would you advise Karthik the next time a post makes him furious?
qa.a: Pause and check the source and data before believing or sharing it, and look for the other side's story.

qa.q: How might Payal feel when Karthik admits she was right?
qa.a: Pleased and respected, and glad the argument led somewhere useful.

grounding: Shows a young adult recognising misinformation and emotional manipulation and seeking out other perspectives.

passage: Darshan, you asked how the job offer went. So, I'm Bhavna, twenty-two, first real job, and the offer came in lower than I'd hoped. My first thought was to just accept it; I didn't want to seem greedy. But I'd read that you should ask for what matters to you. I realised money wasn't my main thing. I'd have a two-hour commute. So I called HR and said, "I'm excited about the role. Could we talk about working from home on Fridays?" They went quiet, then said they'd check. Two days later they agreed, and offered a review after six months. I got what I actually needed, and they got someone who'll stay.

qa.q: What did Bhavna ask HR for?
qa.a: Working from home on Fridays.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling when the offer came in lower than hoped?
qa.a: Bhavna felt disappointed and nervous, worried that asking for more would seem greedy.

qa.q: What made Bhavna's negotiation work?
qa.a: Knowing what mattered most and asking warmly for that, so both sides gained.

qa.q: How might the HR team see Bhavna's request?
qa.a: As reasonable and mature, from someone keen on the role and likely to stay.

grounding: Shows a young adult advocating for real personal needs in a job offer and reaching a compromise.

passage: I'm Gautam, and I share a building with Nikita, twenty-one. Last month our landlord said he'd raise her rent. She'd been complaining for months about the leaking bathroom. She didn't shout. She wrote down every repair she'd asked for, with dates, and went to see him. "I'm happy to stay, and I understand costs go up," she said. "But I'd like the leak fixed first, and a smaller increase until it's done." He argued, then agreed to fix the leak that week and to raise the rent next quarter instead. I don't know how nervous she was, but she came back smiling.

qa.q: What had Nikita been complaining about for months?
qa.a: The leaking bathroom.

qa.q: What might Nikita have felt going to see the landlord?
qa.a: She was probably nervous but prepared, determined to be fair and firm.

qa.q: What made Nikita's approach successful?
qa.a: She came with dates and facts, acknowledged the landlord's side and offered a middle path.

qa.q: How does Gautam see the outcome?
qa.a: Gautam is impressed and notices Nikita came back smiling, though unsure how nervous she was.

grounding: Shows a young adult negotiating calmly with a landlord for a fair compromise, seen by a neighbour.

passage: First month freelancing: Chandrika, twenty, designed a logo for Zubin's café and he asked for changes eleven times. She kept saying yes and felt exhausted. Second month: she wrote a simple agreement for new clients: three rounds of changes included, extra rounds charged, deadlines fixed. Her hands shook when she sent it to Zubin for his next job, a menu. Zubin replied, "Eleven was too many, fair enough. But can we make it four for the menu, since it's bigger?" She agreed. Third month: the menu was done on time, and Zubin recommended her to two other cafés.

qa.q: How many times did Zubin ask for changes to the logo?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when she sent Zubin the agreement?
qa.a: She felt nervous, afraid he might be offended and leave.

qa.q: Which choice made the deal work for both?
qa.a: Setting clear terms and then accepting Zubin's request for four rounds, so both felt respected.

qa.q: How might Zubin see Chandrika after the menu?
qa.a: As a professional he trusts, which is why he recommends her.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to set terms and find a fair compromise with a client over three months.

passage: The train to Bengaluru left in twenty minutes, it was pouring, and Maria, eighteen, was still at the station entrance hugging her brother Varun. Two suitcases, one umbrella, water in her shoes. "You'll be late," he said. "I know." She'd dreamed of this college for two years: her own room, new friends, a city where nobody knew her as "Varun's little sister". And yet her stomach was knotted. What if she hated it? What if nobody liked her? The whistle blew. She laughed and cried at once, grabbed her bags and ran for the train, still waving.

qa.q: How long was it until the train left?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling as she hugged Varun?
qa.a: She felt excited about her new independence and scared about the unknown, both at once.

qa.q: What would you advise Maria for her first weeks?
qa.a: Expect mixed feelings, keep in touch with Varun, and give the new place time before judging it.

qa.q: How might Varun feel watching Maria run for the train?
qa.a: Proud and happy for her, and a bit sad to see her go.

grounding: Shows a young adult holding excitement and fear together as she leaves home for college.

passage: Harish, nineteen, locked the door of his first rented room in Hyderabad and stood in the middle of it. A mattress, a fan, a bucket. Nobody to tell him when to sleep. He put on music loudly, danced a bit, and felt like a king. Then the fan clicked off in a power cut, and the silence was huge. He realised he didn't know where to buy a candle. He called his mother Irawati. "Everything okay?" "Yes. Amazing. Also, where do people buy candles?" She laughed. He laughed too, and felt both free and very small.

qa.q: What was in Harish's first rented room?
qa.a: A mattress, a fan, a bucket.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when he said "Amazing" and asked about candles?
qa.a: He felt thrilled by his freedom and also a little lost and afraid, both at once.

qa.q: What small step helped Harish in the moment?
qa.a: Calling his mother, which let him share both the joy and the worry.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel hearing her son's question?
qa.a: Amused and fond, and quietly reassured that he still calls her.

grounding: Shows a young adult feeling both excitement and fear on his first night living alone.

passage:
"Mummy, I got it. The job in Berlin."
Uma put down her tea. "Aditi! That's wonderful!"
"I know. I screamed in the bathroom."
"Then why are you crying?"
Aditi, twenty-one, wiped her face. "Because I've never been further than Pune. Because I don't speak German. Because you'll be here."
"You wanted this so much."
"I still do. I'm so happy I can't sit still, and so scared I can't sleep."
"Both can be true, beta."
"Can they?"
"When I married and left my village, I felt exactly that." Uma squeezed her hand. "Go. And call every Sunday."

qa.q: What city is the new job in?
qa.a: Berlin.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she said she couldn't sit still or sleep?
qa.a: She felt thrilled about the job and scared about leaving, both at the same time.

qa.q: What did Uma do that helped Aditi?
qa.a: She accepted both feelings, shared her own similar experience and gave her blessing.

qa.q: How might Uma feel about Aditi moving so far?
qa.a: Proud and happy for her daughter, and also sad and a little worried.

grounding: Shows a young adult holding excitement and fear at once about a job abroad, talking it through with her mother.

passage: Sharmila, twenty, came home to Kolkata for the holidays and walked past her old primary school with her childhood friend Payal. The gate was rusted shut; the school had moved. Through the bars they could see the swing they used to fight over, now leaning. "Remember when our biggest problem was who got the window seat?" Payal said. Sharmila laughed, then felt her throat tighten. She missed that feeling of someone else deciding everything, of long afternoons with nothing to fear. And yet, she wouldn't swap her life now. They stood there a long time, then went for phuchka, the same stall, the same uncle.

qa.q: What had happened to the old school's gate?
qa.a: It was rusted shut.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling when her throat tightened?
qa.a: She felt a bittersweet longing for the safety and simplicity of childhood.

qa.q: What would you advise Sharmila about these nostalgic feelings?
qa.a: Enjoy the memories and share them with Payal, while valuing the life she has now.

qa.q: How might Payal feel standing at the gate?
qa.a: Probably the same mix of fondness and sadness, glad to share it with an old friend.

grounding: Shows a young adult's bittersweet longing for childhood when revisiting her old school.

passage:
"Tenzin, are you packing or reading?" Anirban leaned in the doorway.
"Reading. Look, my old comics." Tenzin, twenty-one, held one up. "I read this under the blanket with a torch. Amma never knew."
"She knew."
"She did?"
"She told me. She just let you."
Tenzin smiled. "Life was simple then. No rent, no job interviews, no deciding anything."
"You also cried about maths every night."
"True." He paused. "I sometimes feel angry that it's all so complicated now."
"Everyone does."
Tenzin put the comic in the 'keep' box. "I'm taking this to the new flat."
"Good," said his brother. "For the bad days."

qa.q: Where did Tenzin read the comics as a child?
qa.a: Under the blanket with a torch.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when he said life was simple then?
qa.a: He felt a bittersweet longing for childhood, mixed with some resentment at how complicated life has become.

qa.q: What did Anirban do that helped?
qa.a: He reminded Tenzin that childhood had troubles too, while supporting him in keeping the comic.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt letting Tenzin read under the blanket?
qa.a: Fond and trusting, happy to give him a small secret pleasure.

grounding: Shows a young adult longing for the safety of childhood while packing up his room, with his brother.

passage: I'm Nitin. Last month, at twenty-two, I went back to my grandfather Harish's village for the first time in eight years. The mango tree I used to climb was smaller than I remembered. Or I was bigger. I sat under it and suddenly smelt the same wet earth from the summers when Dada woke me at dawn to steal mangoes from our own tree. Nobody needed anything from me then. No deadlines, no emails, no rent. I felt a pang so strong I had to close my eyes. Dada sat beside me and didn't ask anything. We just listened to the koels.

qa.q: How long had Nitin been away from the village?
qa.a: Eight years.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling, eyes closed under the tree?
qa.a: Nitin felt a strong, bittersweet longing for the carefree safety of childhood summers.

qa.q: What made the moment easier for Nitin?
qa.a: Dada sitting quietly beside him, giving space without questions.

qa.q: How might Dada Harish feel under the old tree beside Nitin?
qa.a: Warm and a little wistful at seeing Nitin there, remembering those summers too.

grounding: Shows a young adult's bittersweet longing for childhood when returning to his grandfather's village.

passage: I'm Karthik. The night before my first job, at twenty-one, I couldn't sleep, and not because I was scared. I lay on my bed in the hostel, grinning at the ceiling. My roommate Hrithik threw a pillow at me. "Stop thinking so loud." But I couldn't. A salary. A desk. A city I'd chosen. I'd already planned the first thing I'd buy for my mother, and which weekend I'd explore the old fort. I ironed my shirt twice. When the alarm went off at six, I was already awake, shoes by the door, ready for my life to start.

qa.q: What did Karthik iron twice?
qa.a: The shirt.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling while grinning at the ceiling?
qa.a: Karthik felt excited and eager about the new job and adult life.

qa.q: What would you advise Karthik to keep that energy going?
qa.a: Enjoy the excitement, but pace the plans so the first weeks don't become overwhelming.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel about Karthik's sleeplessness?
qa.a: Amused and a bit annoyed, but probably happy for Karthik.

grounding: Shows a young adult's forward-looking eagerness on the night before a first job.

passage:
Mentor's note, Afreen, college career cell, May
Sarika (22) came in today to tell me she'd won the fellowship to study water management in the Netherlands. She talked non-stop for twenty minutes, about the course, the canals, the flat she'd share, and the projects she wants to bring back to her district. She had already made a list of questions for the programme office. It was lovely to see. I reminded her to also plan for homesickness and paperwork, and we've booked a session next week to go through her visa checklist.

qa.q: What will Sarika study in the Netherlands?
qa.a: Water management.

qa.q: What does Sarika talking non-stop for twenty minutes suggest?
qa.a: She feels thrilled and eager about the opportunity and the future it opens.

qa.q: Why did Afreen mention homesickness and paperwork?
qa.a: To help Sarika balance her excitement with practical planning.

qa.q: How might Sarika's family feel about the fellowship?
qa.a: Proud and excited, and perhaps a little anxious about her being far away.

grounding: Shows a young adult's eager energy about a fellowship abroad, noted by her mentor.

passage:
Tanvir's diary, Friday
PASSED MY DRIVING TEST. The examiner didn't even look up, just stamped it. I walked out feeling like the whole map had opened. Bhavna and I have been planning a road trip to the hills for a year, and now it's real. Tonight I wrote a list: route, budget, which dhaba does the best parathas. I also want to take Ammi to her sister's village, three hours away, which she hasn't visited in years. I'm nineteen and I have a licence and I can go places. I don't think I've ever looked forward to anything this much.

qa.q: What did Tanvir pass?
qa.a: The driving test.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel walking out after the test?
qa.a: Tanvir felt thrilled and full of eager energy about the freedom ahead.

qa.q: What would you advise Tanvir before the road trip?
qa.a: Plan carefully, drive safely, and maybe do shorter trips first to build confidence.

qa.q: How might Ammi feel about Tanvir's plan to take her to her sister's village?
qa.a: Touched and delighted, looking forward to seeing her sister again.

grounding: Shows a young adult's forward-looking excitement about new adult possibilities after getting a driving licence.

passage: Suraj, you asked why I disappeared for a month. I'm Disha, twenty-two, and when my father had his surgery in March, everything fell on me at once. The hospital forms, the electricity bill, my little brother's school fees, my own job. I'd sit at the table with a pile of papers and just stare. I couldn't start anything. One night I cried in the bathroom for an hour. The next morning, my manager noticed and asked if I was okay. I told her. She gave me two days off, and my aunt came to stay. We made a list together and split it. It's still a lot, but I'm moving again.

qa.q: Who noticed Disha was struggling at work?
qa.a: Her manager.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling while staring at the pile of papers?
qa.a: Disha felt overwhelmed and paralysed, flooded by the sudden weight of responsibilities.

qa.q: What turned things around for Disha?
qa.a: Telling the manager, accepting help from an aunt and splitting the tasks into a list.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel hearing why Disha disappeared?
qa.a: Concerned and sorry, and glad Disha finally shared it.

grounding: Shows a young adult flooded by sudden family responsibilities and finding a way forward with help.

passage: I'm Gurpreet, and I share a flat with my cousin Baljeet. Last week I found him sitting on the kitchen floor, papers all around him: the rent agreement, a tax form, a gas connection letter, his new job's joining documents. He wasn't doing anything, just staring. "I don't even know which one to start," he said. He's twenty-one, and until last month his parents handled all of this. I sat down next to him. We sorted everything into three piles: this week, this month, later. He picked up the top paper from the first pile. It took him ten minutes. Then he picked up the next.

qa.q: How many piles did they sort the papers into?
qa.a: Three piles: this week, this month, later.

qa.q: What might Baljeet have been feeling while staring at the papers?
qa.a: He was probably overwhelmed and frozen by so many new responsibilities at once.

qa.q: Why did sorting into piles help Baljeet?
qa.a: It broke the flood into smaller steps, so he could start with one clear task.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet see Baljeet's situation?
qa.a: Gurpreet understands it's new for him and chooses to help rather than judge.

grounding: Shows a young adult paralysed by sudden adult paperwork and a cousin helping him break it down.

passage: Monday: Lakshmi, twenty-two, started a new job, moved into her first flat and received her first education-loan statement, all in one week. By evening she hadn't unpacked a single box. She ate biscuits for dinner and lay awake. Thursday: her manager, Shalini, noticed her rereading the same email three times. "First week everything?" Lakshmi nodded, eyes stinging. Shalini said, "Write everything down tonight. Circle three things only." The next Monday: Lakshmi had unpacked the kitchen, set up a loan reminder after calling the bank, and circled three new things. It was still a lot. But it had edges now.

qa.q: What did Shalini tell Lakshmi to circle?
qa.a: Three things only.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling as she lay awake on Monday?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and anxious, flooded by too many new responsibilities at once.

qa.q: What small step helped Lakshmi move again?
qa.a: Writing everything down and focusing on three things, so the tasks felt manageable.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel seeing Lakshmi a week later?
qa.a: Relieved and pleased that her simple advice helped.

grounding: Shows a young adult moving from paralysis to action amid a sudden rush of adult responsibilities.

passage: "Tejas, you think this pain will never end? When I, your Manoj Chacha, was twenty-two, I'd prepared for the civil services exam for four years. Everyone in our family believed I'd be an officer. I failed the final interview twice. The second time, I sat on the steps of the exam centre in Delhi until it was dark. It wasn't just the exam. It was the whole life I'd imagined: the uniform, my mother's pride. That life died that day. I grieved it for a year. Then I took a teaching job, just to survive. Now I've taught for thirty years, and some of my students became officers."

qa.q: How many times did young Manoj fail the final interview?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What was young Manoj feeling on the steps of the exam centre?
qa.a: He felt deep sorrow, grieving the whole future he had imagined.

qa.q: What turning point in the story began Manoj's new path?
qa.a: Taking a teaching job after a year of grief, which became his life's work.

qa.q: How might Manoj's mother have felt about his failure?
qa.a: Probably sad for him too, though she may later have been proud of his teaching.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a young adult he grieved the loss of an idealised future.

passage: After five years together, Leela, twenty-two, and her partner had ended it, and she had one rainy Sunday to move out of their shared flat. Her friend Ganga came with a borrowed car. They carried boxes down four flights in the downpour. Leela kept stopping: at the mug they'd bought in Goa, at the plant they'd named. Ganga didn't hurry her. In the car, soaked, Leela finally said, "It's not just him. It's every plan we made. The house, the dog, all of it." Ganga held her hand. "Then grieve all of it. We'll go slow."

qa.q: How many flights of stairs did they carry boxes down?
qa.a: Four flights.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when she stopped at the mug and the plant?
qa.a: She was grieving and heartbroken, for the relationship and for all the future plans that ended with it.

qa.q: What did Ganga do that helped?
qa.a: She stayed patient, didn't rush Leela and let her grieve the whole loss.

qa.q: What is it like for Ganga on that rainy moving day?
qa.a: Tiring and sad, but she chooses to be steady for her friend.

grounding: Shows a young adult grieving the end of a long relationship and the future it held, with a friend's support.

passage: Vasudha, twenty, had danced since she was six. The knee injury came in the final year of college, and the doctor was clear: no professional dancing. For weeks she couldn't even look at her ghungroos. Her friend Zainab visited every Sunday in their Pune hostel and didn't talk about dance unless Vasudha did. One evening Vasudha opened her cupboard, held the ghungroos and cried until her chest hurt. "I didn't just lose dancing," she said. "I lost the person I was going to be." Zainab sat beside her. "You're still her. Just on a different road." Vasudha didn't believe it yet, but she didn't put the ghungroos away.

qa.q: When did Vasudha start dancing?
qa.a: When she was six.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling as she held the ghungroos?
qa.a: She was heartbroken, grieving the future she had imagined as a dancer.

qa.q: What did Zainab do that helped?
qa.a: She visited regularly, followed Vasudha's lead on talking about dance and offered gentle hope.

qa.q: How might Zainab feel watching Vasudha cry?
qa.a: Sad for her friend and wanting to support her without rushing her.

grounding: Shows a young adult grieving the loss of an idealised future after an injury, with a friend's support.

passage: Sumit, you asked how I'm so calm about the move. I'm Irawati, twenty-one. When Papa's shop closed last year, I fought it for months. I kept thinking we could save it, I kept blaming the new mall, I kept pretending it would reopen. Then one night I sat with Papa and saw how tired he was. He said, "Beta, it's over. We start again." Something in me let go. We moved to a smaller flat. I switched to an evening course and a part-time job. It's not what I planned. But fighting it was using all my energy. Now I'm using it for what's next.

qa.q: What did Irawati keep blaming?
qa.a: The new mall.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when something let go?
qa.a: Irawati felt relieved and calmer, finally accepting the loss instead of fighting it.

qa.q: What turning point helped Irawati accept the change?
qa.a: Sitting with Papa, seeing how tired he was and hearing him say it was over.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when he told Irawati it was over?
qa.a: Sad and tired, but also hoping to spare the family more struggle.

grounding: Shows a young adult moving from fighting a hard family change to accepting it.

passage: I'm Shalini, Sahil's older sister. Sahil, twenty, trained for three years to be a pilot. Last month the eye test ruled him out for good. For a week he barely left his room. He kept searching online for exceptions. Then one morning he came to breakfast, ate properly and said, "It's done. I can't change it." He started reading about aircraft engineering instead. He still goes quiet when planes pass overhead. I don't know what he feels in those moments, but he's stopped fighting what can't be changed. Last night he showed me a diagram of a jet engine and explained it for twenty minutes, the way he used to talk about flying.

qa.q: How long did Sahil train to be a pilot?
qa.a: Three years.

qa.q: What might Sahil have been feeling during the week he stayed in his room?
qa.a: He was probably heartbroken and resistant, searching for a way around the result.

qa.q: What would you advise Sahil as he explores aircraft engineering?
qa.a: Talk to people in the field and give himself time to grieve while building a new plan.

qa.q: How does Shalini see Sahil's change?
qa.a: She notices he's accepted the result, though he still goes quiet when planes pass.

grounding: Shows a young adult coming to accept a permanent setback without fighting it, seen by his sister.

passage: January: Noor, nineteen, noticed her grandmother Nirmala forgetting names, and kept correcting her sharply: "Nani, I'm Noor, not Neha!" Nirmala looked hurt and confused. February: the doctor explained what was happening, and that it would not get better. Noor argued with her mother that they should try another doctor, another test. March: one evening Nirmala called her "Neha" again. This time Noor just smiled, sat beside her and said, "Tell me about Neha." Nirmala's face lit up. Noor realised that fighting it had only hurt them both. After that, she learned to follow Nani's stories wherever they went, and to save her own tears for the walk home.

qa.q: What name did Nirmala call Noor by mistake?
qa.a: Neha.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when she kept correcting her grandmother in January?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and scared, refusing to accept the change.

qa.q: What changed in March, and why did it help?
qa.a: Noor stopped correcting and joined Nirmala's world, which brought them both peace.

qa.q: How might Nirmala feel when Noor asks about Neha?
qa.a: Happy and understood, rather than confused and corrected.

grounding: Shows a young adult moving over three months from fighting to accepting a grandmother's decline.

passage:
Dear Nitin Sir,
I got the result today. I failed the second level of the accountancy exam again, by six marks. I cried the whole afternoon. For an hour I thought about giving up and taking any job. But I remembered what you said when I was your student: failure is information. So tonight I went through my paper. I lost most marks in taxation, the same as last time. I'm going to join the weekend batch you recommended and practise a full paper every Sunday. The next attempt is in six months. I'm scared, but I'm trying again.
Dolma

qa.q: By how many marks did Dolma fail?
qa.a: By six marks.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling during that hour of thinking about giving up?
qa.a: Dolma felt deeply discouraged and hurt after failing again.

qa.q: What did Dolma do that shows determination?
qa.a: Dolma studied the paper, found the weak area and made a specific plan for the next attempt.

qa.q: How might Nitin Sir feel reading this email?
qa.a: Moved and proud that a former student is using Sir's own words to try again.

grounding: Shows a young adult building the grit to try again after a significant exam setback.

passage: Swati, thanks for having me on your podcast. So, I'm Kiran, twenty-two, and my first business failed. I started a tiffin service in college with two friends. We had forty customers, then a food-safety complaint, and in two weeks we had none. We closed. I didn't cook for months. I felt like a fraud. Then my younger cousin asked me to make lunch for her hostel room, just once. I did, carefully, properly licensed this time. Now I have a small kitchen and thirty customers. Some days I'm still scared it'll all fall apart. But I'd rather try and fail than not try.

passage: I'm Sahil, Kavitha's brother. Kavitha, twenty, missed selection for the national athletics camp by one place last year. She came home and didn't run for three weeks. Then one morning I heard her shoes on the stairs at five. She'd written a plan on the fridge: strength twice a week, video of every race, rest on Sundays. She found a new coach at the stadium. Some mornings she came back limping and silent. This year she made the camp. I don't know what kept her going on the bad days, but she never missed a five o'clock start.

qa.q: By how many places did Kavitha miss selection?

qa.q: What helped Kavitha succeed the second time?
qa.a: A clear written plan, a new coach and steady early training even on hard days.

qa.q: How does Sahil see his sister's comeback?

grounding: Shows a young adult building grit to try again after a major sporting setback, seen by her brother.

passage: Charu, you asked how I stopped burning out. I'm Sharmila, twenty-two, and by last spring I was working ten hours a day at the firm and answering emails at midnight. I forgot how to laugh. One Sunday my niece made me play a ridiculous board game where you have to act like animals. I did a terrible elephant, and I laughed so hard I cried. I realised I hadn't played in years. So now Sunday mornings are for cycling by the lake, and Wednesday nights are for silly games with friends. Work still matters. But I'm better at it when I've been an elephant.

qa.q: What animal did Sharmila act out?

qa.q: Which changes helped Sharmila balance work and play?

qa.a: Delighted and proud, even without fully understanding why.

grounding: Shows a young adult rediscovering play and hobbies as a counterweight to work stress.

passage: I'm Pema, and I work with Rehana at a design agency. During deadline week, everyone was grim, eating lunch at our desks. On Wednesday Rehana, twenty-two, folded a paper aeroplane from a draft, stood on a chair and announced a flying contest. People groaned, then joined. Our manager's plane won. For ten minutes the whole office laughed. Then everyone went back to work, somehow faster. Someone pinned the winning plane above the printer, and on Friday, when the files finally went out, three people added their own planes beside it. I don't know if she planned it, but the mood lifted for the rest of the week.

passage: Exam month: Rashmi, twenty-one, studied fourteen hours a day, snapped at everyone and stopped answering her friend Pradeep's calls. Two weeks in: Pradeep turned up at her hostel with a cheap karaoke speaker. "One song. Then I leave." She sang, badly, an old film song, and laughed for the first time in days. After exams: they started Friday karaoke nights with friends, off-key and loud. Rashmi noticed she slept better and studied more clearly on Saturdays. "I thought fun was a reward for after," she told Pradeep. "Turns out it's part of the fuel."

qa.q: What did Pradeep bring to Rashmi's hostel?
